forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tunbridge Wells forecasts 2027/28 budget gap of £801,000, down from £4.5m forecast in February
news_drafts.lead:
Tunbridge Wells Borough Council is forecasting a deficit of £801,000 for 2027/28, a budget update before its Cabinet on 22 October shows. In February, the council reported a forecast deficit of £4.5m for the same year to Full Council, so the forecast gap has fallen by about £4.0m.

The update gives two reasons for the change: the council has awarded major contracts, and it has been notified of the Local Government Finance Settlement, the government's annual funding announcement for councils. The paper says the remaining gap will need to be closed through further efficiencies and service changes.

The council's strategy on council tax is to raise it each year up to the referendum threshold, the level above which a council must hold a local vote on an increase. The update says: "This council has historically had a policy of very low council tax levels and the strategy is for council tax to increase up to the threshold for triggering a referendum." It says low existing bills leave room to do this. It also says the government assumes, in its own assessment of the council's finances, that the council will raise council tax by the maximum permitted.

news_drafts.headline: Tunbridge Wells cuts forecast 2027/28 budget gap to £801,000 from £4.5m reported in February
news_drafts.lead:
Tunbridge Wells Borough Council's forecast budget deficit for 2027/28, the gap between what it expects to spend and what it expects to have, has fallen to £801,000. In February the council reported a deficit of £4.5m to Full Council. The new figure is in a budget update going to the council's Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board on 5 October.

The paper gives two reasons for the reduction: the awarding of major contracts, and the council being notified of the Local Government Finance Settlement, the government's annual announcement of funding for councils. The update says a deficit of £801,000 "is currently forecast for 2027/28, a decrease on the £4.5m reported to Full Council in February".

The gap has not yet been closed. The council's directors are continuing work on it through service planning and proposals for efficiencies. Officers are due to report back in December with draft proposals.

news_drafts.headline: Tunbridge Wells council starts year with stronger cash position as investment income outperforms
news_drafts.lead: Tunbridge Wells Cabinet heard on 24 September that the council opened the financial year with £41.9 million in cash, £1.9 million more than budgeted, after capital projects totalling £14.074 million were rescheduled into 2026/27. The stronger liquidity position has boosted investment returns. The council forecasts investment income of £2.2 million for the year against a £2 million budget, a surplus of £200,000 that will be transferred to reserves, after achieving an average interest rate of 4.13 per cent rather than the budgeted 3.94 per cent. Q1 investment balances reached £48.3 million, well above the year-end budget assumption of £28.9 million. The council holds no external debt. However, the capital programme is forecast to spend £19.9 million in 2026/27 against a budget of £8.9 million—more than double—and the Grant Volatility Reserve, which buffers against swings in government funding, is forecast to be completely depleted by March 2027.

findings.headline: Council tax strategy to increase to referendum threshold to help close budget gap
findings.detail: The council's strategy is to increase council tax annually up to the referendum threshold. Given historically low council tax levels compared to other authorities, headroom exists to do this. Government assumes in its financial assessment that the council will increase council tax by the maximum permitted.
findings.matters: Councils relying on council tax increases to close budget gaps must manage impact on residents and balance against public resistance to rises.
findings.figures: Council tax to increase to referendum threshold (percentage varies annually); council has historically low council tax levels with headroom to increase
findings.quote: This council has historically had a policy of very low council tax levels and the strategy is for council tax to increase up to the threshold for triggering a referendum.

findings.headline: Secretary of State reviewing Local Government Reorganisation decision, creating budget and workforce uncertainty
findings.detail: The Secretary of State has decided to review the decision to move forward with a four-unitary model for Kent. The council explicitly identifies LGR uncertainty as the major factor determining the 2027/28 deficit size, and identifies recruitment and staff retention during this disruption as key budget influences. Budget projections are described as remaining fluid.
findings.matters: Reorganisation uncertainty impairs the council's ability to plan, recruit and retain experienced staff, and forecast costs, creating material risk to budget forecasts and service delivery.
findings.figures: Not quantified; identified as major influence over budget deficit determination
findings.quote: The major influence over the size of the budget deficit for 2027/28 will be determined by the level of inflation across the council's cost base and the ability to recruit and retain staff during the disruption and uncertainty around Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Bank of England holding interest rates at 3.75 percent, supporting council investment income
findings.detail: The Bank of England held interest rates at 3.75% at its September 2026 meeting, maintaining rates higher than previously forecast. This is supporting returns on the council's cash balances and management of funds held on behalf of other bodies.
findings.matters: Higher interest rates increase returns on council cash holdings, providing additional investment income to offset budget pressures.
findings.quote: Despite rising inflation The Bank of England held interest rates  to 3.75 per cent at its September meeting. For the Council, interest rates reamaining higher than forecast does have a positive impact on interest earned from balances.

findings.headline: Capital Economics forecasts significantly higher inflation pressures for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's inflation forecasts based on Capital Economics data show forecast increases across RPI, RPIX, CPIH, and CPI for 2027/28 compared to 2026/27. Energy inflation is marked by volatility. These pressures will increase council costs across staffing, supplies, premises, and services.
findings.matters: Higher inflation drives up council costs faster than the council can raise revenue through council tax or government grant, squeezing the budget.
findings.figures: Charts show multiple inflation indices (RPI, RPIX, CPIH, CPI) with 2027/28 forecasts higher than 2026/27; energy inflation (electricity, gas, solid fuels, liquid fuels) showing volatility
findings.quote: Inflation forecast provided by Capital Economics, suggest much higher inflation pressures into 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council holds no external debt, providing flexibility to borrow for capital and operational purposes
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has no external debt, meaning no debt servicing costs or refinancing risk. The s151 Officer retains full flexibility to borrow from the Public Works Loan Board or other sources. The council does hold £4.1m in outstanding financing obligations against specific property assets.
findings.matters: Absence of external debt avoids refinancing risk and rising borrowing cost exposure, and retains full ability to use borrowing as a financing tool.
findings.figures: £0 external debt; £4,128k outstanding financing obligations as of 31-Mar-26
findings.quote: The Council does not have any external debt but, the s151 Officer has the flexibility to borrow where appropriate.

daily_post.headline: Council holds no external debt and is maintaining minimum statutory reserves, demonstrating financial discipline.
daily_post.lead: A council with no external debt has maximum financial flexibility and lower refinancing risk; lenders value borrowing restraint and this is a positive resilience indicator.
